expectedText:
COMMERCIAL LEASE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc.

PARTIES, PREMISES, AND RENT
This is a commercial lease agreement between Acme Properties, LLC ("Landlord") and Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc. ("Tenant") for the commercial premises located at 500 Commerce Way, Suite 200, Springfield. The lease term runs from September 1, 2026 to August 31, 2031. Tenant will pay Landlord base rent of $4,500 per month, due on the day of each month specified in this agreement, payable by the method specified in this agreement. This lease is for commercial, non-residential use of the premises only. It does not create a residential tenancy, and the statutory protections that apply specifically to residential tenancies under California law do not apply to it.

USE OF PREMISES
Tenant may use the premises only for the following purpose(s): General office use (the "Permitted Use"), and for no other purpose without Landlord's prior written consent. Confirming that the Permitted Use complies with applicable zoning, building, health, safety, and accessibility requirements for the premises is Tenant's responsibility.

RESIDENTIAL-ONLY STATUTES DON'T APPLY HERE
California's residential security deposit statute, its statewide just-cause-for-termination rule, and its statewide rent-increase cap each apply only to residential tenancies, not to a commercial lease. Civil Code § 1950.5, the security deposit statute, states that it "applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant." Civil Code §§ 1946.2 (the just-cause termination rule) and 1947.12 (the rent-increase cap) each define their own scope as "residential real property," which both statutes define identically as "any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation." None of these three statutes contains language reaching a commercial tenancy.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(a), California Civil Code, scope of the residential security deposit statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  ""Residential real property" means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(k)(2), California Civil Code, scope of the statewide just-cause statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.2.)
  ""Residential real property" means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12(g)(4), California Civil Code, scope of the statewide rent-cap statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1947.12.)
  Known gap: This document doesn't restate the security-deposit cap, the just-cause termination requirements, or the rent-increase cap found elsewhere in California law, because none of them govern a commercial lease by their own terms — a landlord and tenant negotiating a commercial lease are working from a different, thinner statutory baseline than a residential landlord and tenant. This is one state's statutes; some other states regulate commercial security deposits, commercial eviction notice, or commercial rent increases even though California generally does not for those specific protections (see the separate clauses on security deposits and notice elsewhere in this document for the commercial-specific rules that do exist). Two of the three citations below (§§ 1946.2 and 1947.12) happen to use identical definitional language for "residential real property," but they are independent, separately enacted and amended sections of the code, not subsections of one statute.

NO IMPLIED WARRANTY OF HABITABILITY FOR COMMERCIAL SPACE
California's implied warranty of habitability — the doctrine requiring a landlord to keep leased space fit for occupation — was recognized by the California Supreme Court specifically for residential leases, not commercial ones. Consistent with that, the statutory checklist defining what "habitable" specifically requires (Civil Code § 1941.1) is written in terms of a "dwelling," and the companion statute making the habitability duty non-waivable (Civil Code § 1942.1) is written in terms of "a lessee of a dwelling." Neither statute's text extends to commercial premises.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "each of these jurisdictions has discarded the old common law rule and has adopted an implied warranty of habitability for residential leases... we have determined that the Hinson court properly recognized a common law implied warranty of habitability in residential leases in California..."
  — Green v. Superior Court, 10 Cal. 3d 616 (1974) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1182285/green-v-superior-court/)
  "A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics or is a residential unit described in Section 17920.3 or 17920.10 of the Health and Safety Code..."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a), California Civil Code, the tenantability checklist is dwelling-specific (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  "Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.1, California Civil Code, the non-waiver rule is dwelling-specific (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.1.)
  Known gap: A commercial tenant can't point to a defined statutory habitability checklist the way a residential tenant can. What a commercial space needs to be fit for its intended use is left almost entirely to what the lease itself says — which is why a commercial lease typically carries its own detailed condition-of-premises, maintenance, and repair provisions; state law doesn't fill that gap the way it does for a residential unit. This is one state's case law and statutory scheme, current as of this document's research date; some other states extend habitability-type protections to commercial tenants in narrower circumstances (for example, for latent defects known to the landlord), and this document doesn't track any state but California.

COMMERCIAL SECURITY DEPOSITS ARE REGULATED DIFFERENTLY, NOT LEFT UNREGULATED
Commercial security deposits are governed by a separate, less protective statute than the residential one — Civil Code § 1950.7 — rather than being entirely unregulated. Section 1950.7 doesn't cap the amount a commercial landlord can charge as a deposit, and it doesn't require the itemized statement that Civil Code § 1950.5 requires for a residential deposit. But it does restrict what the deposit can be used for — unpaid rent, repairing tenant-caused damage, and cleaning at the end of the tenancy — and it does set return deadlines: if the landlord's only claim is for possible unpaid rent and the deposit (plus anything designated as last month's rent) is one month's rent or less, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days of the landlord regaining possession; if that rent-only deposit exceeds one month's rent, the excess over one month must be returned within two weeks, with the remainder returned or accounted for within 30 days; and if the landlord's claim includes damage repair or cleaning, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days. A landlord who retains a commercial deposit in bad faith is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus a statutory penalty of up to $200.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Any payment or deposit of money the primary function of which is to secure the performance of a rental agreement for other than residential property or any part of the agreement, other than a payment or deposit, including an advance payment of rent, made to secure the execution of a rental agreement, shall be governed by the provisions of this section. With respect to residential property, the provisions of Section 1950.5 shall prevail."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(a), California Civil Code, scope of the commercial deposit statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.7.)
  "The landlord may claim of the payment or deposit only those amounts as are reasonably necessary to remedy tenant defaults in the payment of rent, to repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, or to clean the premises upon termination of the tenancy, if the payment or deposit is made for any or all of those specific purposes. (1) If the claim of the landlord upon the payment or deposit is only for defaults in the payment of rent and the security deposit equals no more than one month's rent plus a deposit amount clearly described as the payment of the last month's rent, then any remaining portion of the payment or deposit shall be returned to the tenant at a time as may be mutually agreed upon by landlord and tenant, but in no event later than 30 days from the date the landlord receives possession of the premises."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(c), California Civil Code, permitted deductions and return deadlines (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.7.)
  "The bad faith retention by a landlord or transferee of a payment or deposit or any portion thereof, in violation of this section, may subject the landlord or the transferee to damages not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200), in addition to any actual damages."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.7(f), California Civil Code, bad-faith retention penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.7.)
  Known gap: This is worth stating precisely because it corrects a common assumption: California doesn't simply have no rule for commercial security deposits — it has a real statute, just a much thinner one than the residential statute. There is no deposit-amount cap, no photo-documentation duty, no pre-move-out inspection right, and the bad-faith penalty tops out at $200 rather than residential's up-to-double-the-deposit exposure. Because there's no statutory cap on amount, the deposit figure in a commercial lease is set entirely by negotiation. This is one state's statute; other states regulate commercial deposits differently, including some with no statute on the subject at all. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.7) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

CASP INSPECTION STATUS DISCLOSURE
A commercial property owner or lessor must state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether the premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp). If the premises have not been issued a CASp disability access inspection certificate confirming compliance, the lease must include this exact statutory disclosure: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A commercial property owner or lessor shall state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether or not the subject premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(a), California Civil Code, the disclosure obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1938.)
  "If the subject premises have not been issued a disability access inspection certificate, as described in subdivision (e) of Section 55.53, the commercial property owner or lessor shall state the following on the lease form or rental agreement: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises.""
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(e), California Civil Code, the required disclosure paragraph (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1938.)
  "As used in this section, "commercial property" means property that is offered for rent or lease to persons operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation as defined in Section 202 of Chapter 2 of Part 2 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations, or a facility to which the general public is invited, at those premises."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(f), California Civil Code, definition of "commercial property" for this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1938.)
  Known gap: This applies to "commercial property" as this specific statute defines it — property offered for rent to someone operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation, or a facility the general public is invited to — so it's aimed squarely at retail and public-facing space; the statute doesn't itself say whether it reaches every kind of non-public commercial lease (e.g., a private warehouse with no public access), and this document doesn't resolve that line. Separate rules apply if the premises have already been inspected and no impacting alterations have happened since (the CASp report must be shared with a confidentiality agreement, and a 72-hour rescission right applies if it isn't shared at least 48 hours before signing) — this clause's quoted paragraph is specifically for the no-certificate case. This is one state's statute; this particular pre-lease accessibility disclosure requirement is distinctive to California, not a nationwide practice. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

TENANT'S RIGHT TO REQUEST A CASP INSPECTION
Section 1938 doesn't just require a disclosure — it separately protects the tenant's ability to have the premises inspected. Even though state law doesn't require a CASp inspection, the statute states the landlord "may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant." The statute requires the parties to "mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary" — meaning the statute itself does not assign that cost to either party by default; it's left to negotiation. Separately, if a CASp inspection has already happened and turned up violations, the statute presumes the landlord bears the cost of fixing them, "unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(e) [inspection right], California Civil Code, tenant's right to request an inspection and cost/time arrangements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1938.)
  "Making any repairs or modifications necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards that are noted in a CASp report is presumed to be the responsibility of the commercial property owner or lessor, unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1938(c), California Civil Code, default responsibility for repairs found in an existing CASp report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1938.)
  Known gap: The task of confirming "who bears the cost" of a tenant-requested inspection has an honest answer that cuts against a natural assumption: the statute does not say the tenant pays for it. It requires the landlord and tenant to mutually agree on the fee, the timing, and the manner of the inspection — cost-shifting isn't automatic in either direction under this statute. What the statute does presume by default is that the landlord bears the cost of fixing violations an inspection turns up, unless the parties agree otherwise. This is one state's statute. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) as the CASp disclosure clause elsewhere in this document; no additional independent source was found for this.

NOTICE TO END A COMMERCIAL TENANCY
For a periodic (e.g., month-to-month) commercial tenancy with no fixed end date, Civil Code § 1946 sets a default notice period of 30 days from either party to terminate — the same general default statute that applies to any periodic tenancy of real property, residential or commercial, unless the parties agree in the lease to a shorter period (as little as seven days). A narrower statute, Civil Code § 1946.1, extends the longer, residential-style 60-day (or 30-day, for a tenancy under a year) notice period to a "qualified commercial tenant" specifically — defined as a tenant that is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit with fewer than 20 employees, that has given the landlord a required written self-attestation of that status. Outside that narrow category, an ordinary commercial tenant gets the 30-day default under § 1946, not the 60-day residential-style period. For ending a tenancy for cause — nonpayment of rent or a lease breach — the same unlawful detainer statute used for residential tenancies, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161, applies to commercial tenancies too: it requires three days' written notice (excluding judicial holidays) to pay rent or quit, or to cure a covenant breach or quit, before an unlawful detainer action can be filed, because § 1161 applies broadly to "a tenant of real property," not only a residential dwelling unit. California law even sets out a separate set of notice-service methods specifically for a "commercial tenant" under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, confirming the legislature understands this statute to reach commercial tenancies directly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days; provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination. It shall be competent for the parties to provide by an agreement at the time the tenancy is created that a notice of the intention to terminate the same may be given at any time not less than seven days before the expiration of the term thereof."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946, California Civil Code, default 30-day notice to end a periodic tenancy of real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.)
  "An owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 60 days prior to the proposed date of termination. A tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy prior to the proposed date of termination... an owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 30 days prior to the proposed date of termination if a tenant or resident has resided in the dwelling or occupied the property for less than one year."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(b)-(c), California Civil Code, extended 60/30-day notice for a qualified commercial tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.1.)
  ""Qualified commercial tenant" means a tenant of commercial real property that meets both of the following requirements: (A) The tenant is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit organization with fewer than 20 employees. (B) (i) Subject to clause (ii), the tenant has provided the landlord, within the previous 12 months, a written notice that the tenant is a qualified commercial tenant and a self-attestation regarding the number of employees, at such time the protections under this section come into place."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(k)(4), California Civil Code, definition of "qualified commercial tenant" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.1.)
  "When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), Code of Civil Procedure, three-day pay-rent-or-quit notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "As used in this section, "tenant" includes any person who hires real property except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(7), Code of Civil Procedure, this notice statute is not limited to dwellings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "The notices required by Section 1161 may be served upon a commercial tenant by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from the commercial rental property, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at the property, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the address where the property is situated... For purposes of subdivision (b), "commercial tenant" means a person or entity that hires any real property in this state that is not a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code, or a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.3 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(b)-(c), Code of Civil Procedure, separate service methods and definition for a commercial tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1162.)
  Known gap: This describes the statutory floor, not the whole picture — a fixed-term commercial lease typically states its own notice-and-cure terms, and none of this analysis governs a fixed-term lease that simply expires by its own stated end date (though the lease may separately require notice of intent to renew or vacate). Whether a specific tenant actually qualifies as a "qualified commercial tenant" under § 1946.1 depends on facts (entity type, employee count, and whether the required written self-attestation was actually given) that this document doesn't evaluate. This is one state's statutes, current as of a January 1, 2025 amendment that extended § 1946.1 to qualified commercial tenants for the first time — notice requirements for ending a commercial tenancy vary significantly by state, and some states impose no statutory notice floor at all for a commercial periodic tenancy. Two of the citations below (§ 1946.1(b)-(c) and § 1946.1(k)(4)) are subsections of the same statutory section, as are two others (§ 1161(2) and § 1161(7)); together, the citations below draw from four independently enacted statutes — §§ 1946, 1946.1, 1161, and 1162 — not one source restated multiple times.

PERSONAL GUARANTIES ARE GENERAL CONTRACT LAW, NOT A COMMERCIAL-LEASE-SPECIFIC STATUTE
California has no statute written specifically for a personal guaranty of a commercial lease. What applies instead is the general contract-law statute of frauds: Civil Code § 1624(a)(2) makes "a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another" — which is what a personal guaranty of a tenant entity's lease obligations is — unenforceable "unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent." Separately, the lease itself, if for a term longer than one year, independently must be in writing under Civil Code § 1624(a)(3).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent... (2) A special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another, except in the cases provided for in Section 2794."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1624(a)(2), California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a promise to answer for another's debt (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1624.)
  "An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of real property, or of an interest therein; such an agreement, if made by an agent of the party sought to be charged, is invalid, unless the authority of the agent is in writing, subscribed by the party sought to be charged."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1624(a)(3), California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a lease longer than one year (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1624.)
  Known gap: This is an honest gap in the sense the task asked to check for: there is no commercial-lease-specific guaranty statute in California comparable to, say, the CASp disclosure requirement. A personal guaranty of a commercial lease is enforced, or not, under the same general statute-of-frauds and suretyship principles that apply to a personal guaranty of any other kind of debt or obligation — principles found in Civil Code § 1624 and in the general suretyship statutes (Civil Code §§ 2787 et seq.), which this document doesn't otherwise cover. This is one state's statute of frauds; every state has some version of a statute of frauds covering a promise to answer for another's debt, but the exact wording and exceptions vary. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1624) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES
Signed:

Landlord: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Tenant: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Guarantor (if applicable): ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

A personal guaranty of Tenant's obligations under this lease is a separate promise that California law requires to be set out in a signed writing of its own; an individual's signature on this lease in a representative capacity for a business-entity Tenant does not, by itself, create a personal guaranty of that entity's obligations.

expectedJSON.body: Commercial security deposits are governed by a separate, less protective statute than the residential one — Civil Code § 1950.7 — rather than being entirely unregulated. Section 1950.7 doesn't cap the amount a commercial landlord can charge as a deposit, and it doesn't require the itemized statement that Civil Code § 1950.5 requires for a residential deposit. But it does restrict what the deposit can be used for — unpaid rent, repairing tenant-caused damage, and cleaning at the end of the tenancy — and it does set return deadlines: if the landlord's only claim is for possible unpaid rent and the deposit (plus anything designated as last month's rent) is one month's rent or less, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days of the landlord regaining possession; if that rent-only deposit exceeds one month's rent, the excess over one month must be returned within two weeks, with the remainder returned or accounted for within 30 days; and if the landlord's claim includes damage repair or cleaning, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days. A landlord who retains a commercial deposit in bad faith is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus a statutory penalty of up to $200.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the commercial deposit statute
citations.quote: Any payment or deposit of money the primary function of which is to secure the performance of a rental agreement for other than residential property or any part of the agreement, other than a payment or deposit, including an advance payment of rent, made to secure the execution of a rental agreement, shall be governed by the provisions of this section. With respect to residential property, the provisions of Section 1950.5 shall prevail.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, permitted deductions and return deadlines
citations.quote: The landlord may claim of the payment or deposit only those amounts as are reasonably necessary to remedy tenant defaults in the payment of rent, to repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, or to clean the premises upon termination of the tenancy, if the payment or deposit is made for any or all of those specific purposes. (1) If the claim of the landlord upon the payment or deposit is only for defaults in the payment of rent and the security deposit equals no more than one month's rent plus a deposit amount clearly described as the payment of the last month's rent, then any remaining portion of the payment or deposit shall be returned to the tenant at a time as may be mutually agreed upon by landlord and tenant, but in no event later than 30 days from the date the landlord receives possession of the premises.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, bad-faith retention penalty
citations.quote: The bad faith retention by a landlord or transferee of a payment or deposit or any portion thereof, in violation of this section, may subject the landlord or the transferee to damages not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200), in addition to any actual damages.

expectedJSON.gap: This is worth stating precisely because it corrects a common assumption: California doesn't simply have no rule for commercial security deposits — it has a real statute, just a much thinner one than the residential statute. There is no deposit-amount cap, no photo-documentation duty, no pre-move-out inspection right, and the bad-faith penalty tops out at $200 rather than residential's up-to-double-the-deposit exposure. Because there's no statutory cap on amount, the deposit figure in a commercial lease is set entirely by negotiation. This is one state's statute; other states regulate commercial deposits differently, including some with no statute on the subject at all. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.7) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: A commercial property owner or lessor must state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether the premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp). If the premises have not been issued a CASp disability access inspection certificate confirming compliance, the lease must include this exact statutory disclosure: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the disclosure obligation
citations.quote: A commercial property owner or lessor shall state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether or not the subject premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the required disclosure paragraph
citations.quote: If the subject premises have not been issued a disability access inspection certificate, as described in subdivision (e) of Section 55.53, the commercial property owner or lessor shall state the following on the lease form or rental agreement: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."

citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "commercial property" for this section
citations.quote: As used in this section, "commercial property" means property that is offered for rent or lease to persons operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation as defined in Section 202 of Chapter 2 of Part 2 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations, or a facility to which the general public is invited, at those premises.

expectedJSON.gap: This applies to "commercial property" as this specific statute defines it — property offered for rent to someone operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation, or a facility the general public is invited to — so it's aimed squarely at retail and public-facing space; the statute doesn't itself say whether it reaches every kind of non-public commercial lease (e.g., a private warehouse with no public access), and this document doesn't resolve that line. Separate rules apply if the premises have already been inspected and no impacting alterations have happened since (the CASp report must be shared with a confidentiality agreement, and a 72-hour rescission right applies if it isn't shared at least 48 hours before signing) — this clause's quoted paragraph is specifically for the no-certificate case. This is one state's statute; this particular pre-lease accessibility disclosure requirement is distinctive to California, not a nationwide practice. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1938 doesn't just require a disclosure — it separately protects the tenant's ability to have the premises inspected. Even though state law doesn't require a CASp inspection, the statute states the landlord "may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant." The statute requires the parties to "mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary" — meaning the statute itself does not assign that cost to either party by default; it's left to negotiation. Separately, if a CASp inspection has already happened and turned up violations, the statute presumes the landlord bears the cost of fixing them, "unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant."

citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's right to request an inspection and cost/time arrangements
citations.quote: the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, default responsibility for repairs found in an existing CASp report
citations.quote: Making any repairs or modifications necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards that are noted in a CASp report is presumed to be the responsibility of the commercial property owner or lessor, unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant.

expectedJSON.gap: The task of confirming "who bears the cost" of a tenant-requested inspection has an honest answer that cuts against a natural assumption: the statute does not say the tenant pays for it. It requires the landlord and tenant to mutually agree on the fee, the timing, and the manner of the inspection — cost-shifting isn't automatic in either direction under this statute. What the statute does presume by default is that the landlord bears the cost of fixing violations an inspection turns up, unless the parties agree otherwise. This is one state's statute. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) as the CASp disclosure clause elsewhere in this document; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: For a periodic (e.g., month-to-month) commercial tenancy with no fixed end date, Civil Code § 1946 sets a default notice period of 30 days from either party to terminate — the same general default statute that applies to any periodic tenancy of real property, residential or commercial, unless the parties agree in the lease to a shorter period (as little as seven days). A narrower statute, Civil Code § 1946.1, extends the longer, residential-style 60-day (or 30-day, for a tenancy under a year) notice period to a "qualified commercial tenant" specifically — defined as a tenant that is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit with fewer than 20 employees, that has given the landlord a required written self-attestation of that status. Outside that narrow category, an ordinary commercial tenant gets the 30-day default under § 1946, not the 60-day residential-style period. For ending a tenancy for cause — nonpayment of rent or a lease breach — the same unlawful detainer statute used for residential tenancies, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161, applies to commercial tenancies too: it requires three days' written notice (excluding judicial holidays) to pay rent or quit, or to cure a covenant breach or quit, before an unlawful detainer action can be filed, because § 1161 applies broadly to "a tenant of real property," not only a residential dwelling unit. California law even sets out a separate set of notice-service methods specifically for a "commercial tenant" under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, confirming the legislature understands this statute to reach commercial tenancies directly.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, default 30-day notice to end a periodic tenancy of real property
citations.quote: A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days; provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination. It shall be competent for the parties to provide by an agreement at the time the tenancy is created that a notice of the intention to terminate the same may be given at any time not less than seven days before the expiration of the term thereof.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, extended 60/30-day notice for a qualified commercial tenant
citations.quote: An owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 60 days prior to the proposed date of termination. A tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy prior to the proposed date of termination... an owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 30 days prior to the proposed date of termination if a tenant or resident has resided in the dwelling or occupied the property for less than one year.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "qualified commercial tenant"
citations.quote: "Qualified commercial tenant" means a tenant of commercial real property that meets both of the following requirements: (A) The tenant is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit organization with fewer than 20 employees. (B) (i) Subject to clause (ii), the tenant has provided the landlord, within the previous 12 months, a written notice that the tenant is a qualified commercial tenant and a self-attestation regarding the number of employees, at such time the protections under this section come into place.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, three-day pay-rent-or-quit notice
citations.quote: When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, this notice statute is not limited to dwellings
citations.quote: As used in this section, "tenant" includes any person who hires real property except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, separate service methods and definition for a commercial tenant
citations.quote: The notices required by Section 1161 may be served upon a commercial tenant by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from the commercial rental property, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at the property, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the address where the property is situated... For purposes of subdivision (b), "commercial tenant" means a person or entity that hires any real property in this state that is not a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code, or a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.3 of the Civil Code.

expectedJSON.gap: This describes the statutory floor, not the whole picture — a fixed-term commercial lease typically states its own notice-and-cure terms, and none of this analysis governs a fixed-term lease that simply expires by its own stated end date (though the lease may separately require notice of intent to renew or vacate). Whether a specific tenant actually qualifies as a "qualified commercial tenant" under § 1946.1 depends on facts (entity type, employee count, and whether the required written self-attestation was actually given) that this document doesn't evaluate. This is one state's statutes, current as of a January 1, 2025 amendment that extended § 1946.1 to qualified commercial tenants for the first time — notice requirements for ending a commercial tenancy vary significantly by state, and some states impose no statutory notice floor at all for a commercial periodic tenancy. Two of the citations below (§ 1946.1(b)-(c) and § 1946.1(k)(4)) are subsections of the same statutory section, as are two others (§ 1161(2) and § 1161(7)); together, the citations below draw from four independently enacted statutes — §§ 1946, 1946.1, 1161, and 1162 — not one source restated multiple times.

expectedJSON.body: California has no statute written specifically for a personal guaranty of a commercial lease. What applies instead is the general contract-law statute of frauds: Civil Code § 1624(a)(2) makes "a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another" — which is what a personal guaranty of a tenant entity's lease obligations is — unenforceable "unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent." Separately, the lease itself, if for a term longer than one year, independently must be in writing under Civil Code § 1624(a)(3).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a promise to answer for another's debt
citations.quote: The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent... (2) A special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another, except in the cases provided for in Section 2794.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a lease longer than one year
citations.quote: An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of real property, or of an interest therein; such an agreement, if made by an agent of the party sought to be charged, is invalid, unless the authority of the agent is in writing, subscribed by the party sought to be charged.

expectedJSON.gap: This is an honest gap in the sense the task asked to check for: there is no commercial-lease-specific guaranty statute in California comparable to, say, the CASp disclosure requirement. A personal guaranty of a commercial lease is enforced, or not, under the same general statute-of-frauds and suretyship principles that apply to a personal guaranty of any other kind of debt or obligation — principles found in Civil Code § 1624 and in the general suretyship statutes (Civil Code §§ 2787 et seq.), which this document doesn't otherwise cover. This is one state's statute of frauds; every state has some version of a statute of frauds covering a promise to answer for another's debt, but the exact wording and exceptions vary. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1624) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

A personal guaranty of Tenant's obligations under this lease is a separate promise that California law requires to be set out in a signed writing of its own; an individual's signature on this lease in a representative capacity for a business-entity Tenant does not, by itself, create a personal guaranty of that entity's obligations.
